## 🌟 Summary
A reliability-focused release with an important TIFF-reading fix, plus improvements to segmentation prompts, model loading, validation, integrations, and Platform workflows—without introducing a new model architecture.

## 📊 Key Changes
- **Multi-page TIFF handling (PR #26842):** By default, grayscale TIFF scans now load as their first page instead of incorrectly combining pages into image channels. Only `cv2.IMREAD_UNCHANGED` stacks same-size pages, preserving the option for multispectral workflows.
- **More reliable YOLOE and YOLO-World loading:** Checkpoint type now determines the correct model wrapper, so specialized models continue to work when saved under generic filenames such as `best.pt`. Changing class names on a text-fused YOLOE model now raises a clear error instead of silently relabeling predictions or failing later.
- **More faithful SAM mask refinement:** Floating-point prompt masks retain negative and fractional values, avoiding unintended changes to mask-refinement inputs.
- **Improved data and metric handling:** Fixes cover multipart polygon connections, confusion-matrix matching, classification prediction with rectangular image sizes, and validation on datasets without labels. Dataset downloads also recognize archive URLs with query strings.
- **Smoother integrations and runtime behavior:** Weights & Biases now supports training inside a user-started run, preserving its settings and leaving it open afterward. Additional fixes improve Platform training resume behavior and OpenVINO/LiteRT device handling.
- **Updated CI and documentation:** CPU runners gain SSH, `rsync`, and libraries needed to import GUI OpenCV. Documentation clarifies Platform dataset workflows and training features, corrects export examples, and refreshes several guides and screenshots.

## 🎯 Purpose & Impact
- **Prevents TIFF-related training failures:** Scanned documents are no longer mistaken for multi-channel images or allowed to produce images with excessive channel counts. Users who intentionally need TIFF pages as bands should use `cv2.IMREAD_UNCHANGED`.
- **Makes model and data workflows more predictable:** Correct model selection, clearer YOLOE class-change errors, and more accurate mask and polygon handling reduce confusing failures and incorrect results.
- **Improves validation and experiment tracking:** Label-free validation avoids unnecessary warnings, confusion-matrix matching is more consistent, and existing W&B runs retain their history and remain available for further logging.
- **Reduces setup friction:** More complete CPU runners and clearer Platform and export documentation make common CI and training tasks easier to run.

### Breaking

* [BUG FIX] Support plain torch tensors and closed-loop policies in differentiable simulation. (@Kashu7100) (#3586)
* [MISC] Get rid of custom Genesis tensor used for differentiable simulation. (@duburcqa) (#3592)

* Fix the incremental Hessian update of the rigid constraint solver on AMDGPU.  (@yugeng-tju) (#3537)
* Fix scene build and shared memory occupancy model on AMD GPUs. (@LuoShaoyinn) (#3545)

* Scale primitive geometry correctly by legacy URDF parser. (@Milotrince) (#3465)
* Drop torch compile that is causing side-effects without performance benefits. (@duburcqa) (#3527)

### Miscellaneous

* Speed up collision detection on scenes with many collision geometries. (@duburcqa) (#3579)
* Speed up collision detection of non-convex meshes. (@duburcqa) (#3583, #3584, #3587, #3588)
* Speed up compilation of rigid collision detection. (@duburcqa) (#3555, #3556)
* Speed up trajectory recording on CPU and GPU. (@duburcqa) (#3538)
* Speed up rebuilding a scene from the same assets. (@Milotrince) (#3392)
* Speed up rebuilding an interactive scene. (@Milotrince) (#3501)
* Improve contact accuracy and reduce collision overhead. (@duburcqa) (#3546, #3554)
* Reduce memory footprint of scenes loading the same asset multiple times. (@duburcqa) (#3568)
* Persistent compiled kernels across sessions. (@duburcqa) (#3551)
* Record trajectories without stalling the simulation, with the timings of every step. (@duburcqa) (#3528)
* Support exporting python scalar in checkpoints and trajectories.  (@duburcqa) (#3531)
* Add new fast trajectory recording mode for batched GPU simulation. (@duburcqa) (#3534)

* Keep the cached data of a scene across an interactive rebuild. (@duburcqa) (#3575)
* Fix spurious warning on scene reset with threaded recorders. (@Nas01010101) (#3574)

summary: At a glance Brings rich interactivity to AI-generated charts: Flint-interactive enables agents to create data visualizations that users can explore directly through clicking, filtering, zooming, highlighting, and cross-chart interactions. Makes complex interactions easier to build: Instead of requiring low-level visualization code, Flint-interactive lets users and agents define behaviors using high-level semantic events and update operators. Improves reliability and reduces development effort: By using Flint’s compiler to handle interaction logic and visual dependencies, the system helps avoid many of the layout, rendering, and debugging challenges common in custom interactive visualizations. Connects charts, text, tables, and applications: Flint-interactive supports interactive data stories, dashboards, and connected experiences where actions in one view can update charts, documents, widgets, or application state in another. AI agents make it easy to analyze data and generate reports with data visualizations. They help users examine patterns more efficiently than by reading verbose text. However, when we’re feeling exploratory, we want to go beyond static visualizations.: We want to interact with charts to zoom in on details, compare data across charts, or even highlight related text in the document from a chart selection, and vice versa. This requires agents to be able to create interactive data visualizations that communicate information while letting readers explore beyond the author’s chosen view, ideally with the quality of interactive stories in sophisticated data journalism. This leaves us wondering: (As a user) Can I interact with charts directly in chat to explore the data and ask follow-up questions based on what I select? (As a developer) Can I enable the AI agents I build for my customers to generate interactive visualizations that help them explore and understand their data? Yes, it’s possible, but there is a significant practical gap. Even with capable frontier models, we still face: High generation cost. Agents rarely produce a fully satisfactory interactive visualization in one turn. Repeated rounds of reasoning, coding, and debugging consume tokens and time. Reliability. Interactive visualizations are challenging enough that expressive interactive charts introduce poor layouts or broken interactions easily, and we risk introducing new problems when trying to fix them. These challenges help explain why consistently generating high-quality interactive visualizations remain difficult in real-world use. Meanwhile, built-in interactions in some visualization libraries are not expressive enough on their own to create bespoke interactive charts. And these challenges are results of the lack of an expressive yet high-level language to specify visual interactions. PODCAST SERIES AI Testing and Evaluation: Learnings from Science and Industry Discover how Microsoft is learning from other domains to advance evaluation and testing as a pillar of AI governance. Listen now Opens in a new tab Flint-interactive Flint-interactive (opens in new tab) is a language for creating interactive data visualizations on top of Flint. It allows users to create dashboards, data stories, and interactive artifacts more easily. The power of Flint-interactive comes from Flint’s compiler, which translates user interactions into semantic events that capture the meaning behind what users select. It then uses high-level operators to update visualizations in response to those events, making sophisticated interactions far easier to create and maintain. This shifts the heavy burden of resolving complex dependencies between interaction and visual logic to the compiler, so the user (or the agent) can easily describe expressive interactions with high-level specifications. Example 1: We can enable the user to brush one visual view, and the chart highlights all groups of country selected by the user with a simple preset interaction linked-brush. How to use 1. Use Flint in your chat Use Flint Interactive directly in your chat or canvas environment through Flint-MCP and MCP Apps, following the MCP setup guide. With the latest release, tell your agent what to chart and which interactions you want; it can generate an interaction_spec alongside the Flint chart spec and render the interactive chart in your conversation. Example 2: Using Flint-interactive in the chat environment, allowing the agent to produce interactive charts more reliably with simple Flint specifications. It also enables the user to select and pass context to the follow-up turns. 2. Build an interactive app with Flint Build interactive charts in a dashboard, data story, or other application with Flint Interactive Canvas. Your app can use event handlers to process semantic events emitted by Flint Canvas, for example to filter a table, update another chart, or change application state. To let your app’s widgets control how the chart updates, send update operators to Flint Canvas. Example 2: Flint-interactive allows developers to define interactions between charts and external elements (e.g., table, paragraph). Here, the user can click the table to highlight points in the chart and verse versa. 3. Create bespoke interactions To create bespoke interactions beyond Flint’s presets, define a trigger and a custom handle function with the programming API that maps semantic events to custom chart update sequences. For example, a handler can highlight a clicked country and label it by name. It combines set-style and set-annotation without manipulating renderer-specific marks. Example 4: The agent can create bespoke interactive visualizations with Flint’s programming API. In this DimpVis example, the user can drag the point along the time path to visualize how all cities’ temperature and precipitation changes. How it works Flint Canvas is a state machine that tracks user interactions on the canvas and manages visual rendering state. Flint makes interaction specification easy by separating visual logic, managed by the compiler, from interaction logic, specified by the user at the semantic level: Visual logic: The compiler automatically resolves raw triggers, such as clicks, drags, and key presses, into semantic events that identify chart elements and data. It also translates update operators into rendered canvas changes, handling hit testing, and low-level visual updates. Interaction logic: The user specifies interactions by mapping semantic interaction events to chart update operators, such as set style to highlight data, set annotation to label a point, or set viewport to pan or zoom. The user can also use those semantic events to update external tables, widgets, or application states. Figure 1: Flint interactive allows the agent to describe interaction logic by mapping “what semantic event is the user interacting with” to “what updates they want for the canvas surface”. The compiler takes the heavy lifting of resolving visual updates and manages the runtime, which makes interaction authoring more reliable c and cost effective. This separation means users do not need to reverse-engineer rendering logic or manipulate renderer-specific marks, making interactions easier to specify and maintain. Furthermore, because event generation and visual updates are compositional, the same model also connects Flint with tables, text, other charts, and widgets to build interactive stories and dashboards. Try it now! Chart users: Set up Flint in your chat (opens in new tab) and ask your agent to create an interactive chart. Find inspiration in the interaction gallery. App builders: Build interactive dashboards, data stories, and connected views with the programming API (opens in new tab). Share the interaction-author skill with your coding agent to add presets to your app. Interaction designers: Explore the bespoke examples (opens in new tab), design a new interaction, and turn it into a reusable preset. Propose a preset on GitHub and share your prototype or implementation to help expand Flint’s interaction vocabulary.
